title: Fox Farm (Mason County)
summary: In Mason County, Fort Ancient farmers lived at Fox Farm from about 1300 into the mid-1600s, one of the longest-lived villages of its kind.
bodyMarkdown:
Fox Farm is a large Fort Ancient village site in Mason County, in northern Kentucky. Native farmers lived there for a long time, and the village changed as it grew. It is one of the better-studied Fort Ancient sites in the state.

## Setting

The [Kentucky Archaeological Survey's Fox Farm page](https://archaeology.ky.gov/Find-a-Site/Pages/Fox-Farm.aspx) describes a village placed where two natural regions meet. Fort Ancient communities often chose such edges because they offered several kinds of resources close together.

Residents cleared land to plant corn, beans and squash. Nearby woods supplied wild plant foods and timber for building, heating and cooking. An account of [Fox Farm site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Farm_site_%28Mays_Lick,_Kentucky%29) says it covers 10 to 16 hectares, with midden deposits up to 80 centimeters thick.

## How long people lived there

The sources give different dates for the village. One account, from the archaeology survey, says Native farmers lived there from 1300 to at least 1650 AD. Another assigns it to the Middle Fort Ancient Manion phase, about 1200 to 1400 CE. Both describe a long-lived village.

The survey ties its unusual length of occupation partly to how residents managed their local environment.

## A growing village

At first, houses formed a ring around a central plaza. As more people moved in, the plan changed to clusters of houses around a large public building. Houses also grew, from about 16.5 by 16.5 feet to 19.9 by 33 feet and finally to 26.4 by 59.4 feet. Floor space rose from 272 to 653 to 1,568 square feet.

More people meant more mouths to feed, and residents changed how they hunted. The survey says they took about twice as many male turkeys as female turkeys. That pattern may have helped keep a healthy wild turkey population near the village.

## An offering in a house wall

One of the site's most unusual finds was a group of 11 deer jaws inside a house wall. Seven were left jaws and four were right, from at least eight deer. The deer had died in different seasons, from spring to winter, so they were not taken in a single hunt.

The bones show no gnawing or weathering. That suggests people kept them for a long time before placing them in the ground. A piece of a pottery jar found with the jaws may have served as a tray to carry them. Because the jaws lay along the outer edge of the house basin, archaeologists think the offering was made when the house was last rebuilt.

## Kentucky today

Fox Farm was added to the National Register of Historic Places on May 9, 1983. The archaeology survey does not publish site locations, and this story gives the county only. Related Fort Ancient stories include the [Buckner site](/stories/buckner-site-fort-ancient-villages-on-strodes-creek/), the [Cleek-McCabe village](/stories/cleek-mccabe-a-circular-fort-ancient-village-in-boone-county/) and [Lower Shawneetown](/stories/lower-shawneetown-at-the-scioto-mouth/). The village was home to Native farmers for generations and deserves respect.
